title: Lucky to bear it
hook: not "I'm unlucky," but "I'm lucky to bear this without breaking" (Meditations 4.49)

segments.voice: Yesterday: the headland. Your line was the headland. When a wave hit, did you stand still and let it settle? Day five hundred sixty-one.

Listen to how people tell bad news. Of course it happened to me. Just my luck. Why does this always happen to me? The sentence starts before we've even decided what we think. It's almost a reflex, a little story about being the unlucky one. Yesterday Marcus Aurelius gave us the headland. In the same entry, a few lines later, he catches himself in exactly that reflex, and rewrites the sentence. Same event. Different words. And the new words change what the event is. Today: lucky to bear it.
screen: `JUST MY LUCK.` → `A REFLEX SENTENCE.` → `LUCKY TO BEAR IT.`

segments.voice: First, the rewrite. Unlucky me, that this happened, Marcus imagines saying. Then he corrects himself. Not at all. Rather: lucky me, that though this happened, I'm still standing, not crushed by the present and not afraid of what's coming. Second, why that's luck. Something like this could have happened to anyone, he says. But not everyone would have come through it unbroken. So why call the event bad luck, rather than calling your steadiness good luck? Both are true. You get to choose which one is the headline. Third, the test. Then he asks the question that matters most. Does what happened stop you from being just, generous, self-controlled, sensible, careful in judgment, honest, modest, free? If it doesn't touch those, it hasn't touched what makes you who you are. Fourth, the rule to carry. Marcus ends with a sentence for every future vexation. Remember, he says: this is not a misfortune, but bearing it well is good fortune. This is not pretending. Marcus doesn't call the loss a gain. He doesn't say it didn't hurt. He moves the word luck from the event, which you didn't choose, to the bearing, which you did. That's a real shift, and anyone can try it. The flat tire is a flat tire. Changing it calmly, on the shoulder, in the rain, without taking it out on anyone: that's the part that's yours, and it's a kind of luck to be able to.
screen: `NOT UNLUCKY ME: LUCKY ME.` · `ANYONE COULD MEET IT; NOT ALL BEAR IT.` · `DOES IT STOP YOU BEING JUST?` · `BEARING IT WELL IS GOOD FORTUNE.` · then, large: `LUCKY TO BEAR IT.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one misfortune, recent or old. Say the reflex sentence to yourself first: just my luck, or why me. Notice how it feels. Now try Marcus's rewrite: this happened, and I'm still standing. Then ask his test: did it stop me from being fair, honest, kind? If not, say quietly: lucky to bear it. Notice whether anything in your body changes. The bell holds the time.
Lucky to bear it. Marcus moves luck from the event to the bearing: this isn't misfortune, but to bear it well is good fortune. Today's word.
Your line: lucky to bear it. The next time you hear yourself say just my luck, rephrase it: this happened, and I'm lucky to bear it well. Day five hundred sixty-one.

howItsDone: Readers of Marcus Aurelius often apply the rule at the end of Meditations 4.49 to setbacks: the event is not a misfortune, but bearing it well is good fortune.

trapdoor: what you thought: look on the bright side.
what it means: luck belongs not to the event but to how you bear it.
what a scholar hears: eutyches against atyches, lucky against unlucky; the Stoics held that only the bearing, not the event, is truly good or bad.

notes: 4.49 paraphrased (second half): 'Unhappy am I, because this has happened to me. Not so, but happy am I, though this has happened, because I continue free from pain, neither crushed by the present nor fearing the future'; such a thing might happen to every man, but not every man would have continued free from pain; will this prevent you being just, magnanimous, temperate, prudent, secure against inconsiderate opinions and falsehood, modest, free? Remember: this is not a misfortune, but to bear it nobly is good fortune. Confirm.
